claim: Muscle regeneration is a complex process due to dynamic and multiscale biochemical and cellular interactions.
source: Muscle regeneration is a complex process due to dynamic and multiscale biochemical and cellular interactions, making it difficult to identify microenvironmental conditions that are beneficial to muscle recovery from injury using experimental approaches alone.
evidence: This is a general characterization statement in the abstract that frames the motivation for the study.

claim: The agent-based model was developed using the Cellular-Potts framework to simulate the dynamic microenvironment of a cross-section of murine skeletal muscle tissue.
source: To understand the degree to which individual cellular behaviors impact endogenous mechanisms of muscle recovery, we developed an agent-based model (ABM) using the Cellular-Potts framework to simulate the dynamic microenvironment of a cross-section of murine skeletal muscle tissue.
evidence: The authors directly state the development of the model and the framework used.

claim: More than 100 published studies were referenced to define over 100 parameters and rules in the model.
source: We referenced more than 100 published studies to define over 100 parameters and rules that dictate the behavior of muscle fibers, satellite stem cells (SSCs), fibroblasts, neutrophils, macrophages, microvessels, and lymphatic vessels, as well as their interactions with each other and the microenvironment.
evidence: The authors explicitly state the number of studies and parameters used in model development.

claim: The model includes muscle fibers, satellite stem cells, fibroblasts, neutrophils, macrophages, microvessels, and lymphatic vessels.
source: We referenced more than 100 published studies to define over 100 parameters and rules that dictate the behavior of muscle fibers, satellite stem cells (SSCs), fibroblasts, neutrophils, macrophages, microvessels, and lymphatic vessels, as well as their interactions with each other and the microenvironment.
evidence: The authors list the cell types included in the model.

claim: Parameter density estimation was utilized to calibrate the model to temporal biological datasets describing cross-sectional area recovery, SSC, and fibroblast cell counts at multiple timepoints following injury.
source: We utilized parameter density estimation to calibrate the model to temporal biological datasets describing cross-sectional area (CSA) recovery, SSC, and fibroblast cell counts at multiple timepoints following injury.
evidence: The authors describe the calibration methodology and the datasets used.

claim: The calibrated model was validated by comparison of macrophage, neutrophil, and capillaries counts to experimental observations.
source: The calibrated model was validated by comparison of other model outputs (macrophage, neutrophil, and capillaries counts) to experimental observations.
evidence: The authors state the validation approach and the metrics used.

claim: Predictions for eight model perturbations were compared to published experimental studies to validate model predictive capabilities.
source: Predictions for eight model perturbations that varied cell or cytokine input conditions were compared to published experimental studies to validate model predictive capabilities.
evidence: The authors describe the validation of predictive capabilities through perturbation studies.

claim: Latin hypercube sampling and partial rank correlation coefficient were used to identify in silico perturbations of cytokine diffusion coefficients and decay rates to enhance CSA recovery.
source: We used Latin hypercube sampling and partial rank correlation coefficient to identify in silico perturbations of cytokine diffusion coefficients and decay rates to enhance CSA recovery.
evidence: The authors describe the sensitivity analysis methods used.

claim: Combined alterations of specific cytokine decay and diffusion parameters result in greater fibroblast and SSC proliferation compared to individual perturbations with a 13% increase in CSA recovery compared to unaltered regeneration at 28 days.
source: This analysis suggests that combined alterations of specific cytokine decay and diffusion parameters result in greater fibroblast and SSC proliferation compared to individual perturbations with a 13% increase in CSA recovery compared to unaltered regeneration at 28 days.
evidence: The authors report the quantitative results of the combined cytokine perturbation analysis.

claim: Skeletal muscle injuries account for more than 30% of all injuries.
source: Skeletal muscle injuries account for more than 30% of all injuries and are one of the most common complaints in orthopedics (Quintero et al., 2009; Barroso and Thiele, 2011; Valle, 2011).
evidence: The authors cite published studies to support this epidemiological claim.

claim: Standard treatment for muscle injuries is limited mostly to rest, ice, compression, elevation, anti-inflammatory drugs, and immobilization.
source: The standard treatment for muscle injuries is limited mostly to rest, ice, compression, elevation, anti-inflammatory drugs, and immobilization (Quintero et al., 2009).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this clinical practice claim.

claim: Standard treatments for muscle injuries lack a firm scientific basis and have varied outcomes, some resulting in incomplete functional recovery, formation of scar tissue, and high injury recurrence rates.
source: These treatments lack a firm scientific basis and have varied outcomes, some resulting in incomplete functional recovery, formation of scar tissue, and high injury recurrence rates (Järvinen et al., 2007; Huard et al., 2022).
evidence: The authors cite published studies to support this claim about treatment outcomes.

claim: Muscle regeneration requires an abundance of cells and cytokines to interact in a highly coordinated mechanism involving five interrelated cascading phases including degeneration, inflammation, regeneration, remodeling, and functional recovery.
source: Muscle regeneration requires an abundance of cells and cytokines to interact in a highly coordinated mechanism involving five interrelated cascading phases including degeneration, inflammation, regeneration, remodeling, and functional recovery (Forcina et al., 2020).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this description of the regeneration process.

claim: Following an acute muscle injury, there is a time-dependent recruitment of neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages to remove necrotic tissue and release factors that regulate fibroblast behavior and SSC activation, proliferation, and division.
source: Following an acute muscle injury, there is a time-dependent recruitment of neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages to remove necrotic tissue and release factors that regulate fibroblast behavior and SSC activation, proliferation, and division (Howard et al., 2020).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this description of the inflammatory response.

claim: Following initial inflammatory response, fibroblasts and SSCs activate and proliferate with the macrophages shifting from their pro- to anti-inflammatory phenotype.
source: Following initial inflammatory response, fibroblasts and SSCs activate and proliferate with the macrophages shifting from their pro- to anti-inflammatory phenotype.
evidence: This is a general description of the regeneration process based on established knowledge.

claim: In healthy muscle, the regeneration process is followed by remodeling where fibroblasts apoptose and SSCs differentiate and fuse to repair the myofibers.
source: In healthy muscle, this process would be followed by remodeling of the muscle where the fibroblasts apoptose and SSCs differentiate and fuse to repair the myofibers (Westman et al., 2021).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this description of the remodeling phase.

claim: The molecular events implicated in angiogenesis occur at early stages of muscle regeneration to restore microvascular networks that are crucial for successful muscle recovery.
source: It has also been shown that the molecular events implicated in angiogenesis occur at early stages of muscle regeneration to restore microvascular networks that are crucial for successful muscle recovery (Wagatsuma, 2007).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this claim about angiogenesis timing.

claim: Cytokines play key roles in dictating cell behaviors and are major drivers of the regeneration cascade.
source: These cytokines play key roles in dictating cell behaviors and are major drivers of the regeneration cascade (Husmann et al., 1996).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this claim about cytokine function.

claim: Testing alterations in cytokine dynamics experimentally has proven to be complex and expensive due to difficulties in cytokine identification and quantification as well as confounding factors due to pleiotropic activities of cytokines and interactions with soluble receptors.
source: Testing alterations in cytokine dynamics experimentally has proven to be complex and expensive due to difficulties in cytokine identification and quantification as well as confounding factors due to pleiotropic activities of cytokines and interactions with soluble receptors (Ciano-Petersen et al., 2022).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this claim about experimental challenges.

claim: There are over a million possible combinations of cytokine alterations, making it unrealistic to study all combinations with experiments alone.
source: There are over a million possible combinations of cytokine alterations, making it unrealistic to study all combinations with experiments alone.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the combinatorial nature of cytokine interactions.

claim: Previous agent-based models of muscle regeneration employed simplistic, non-spatial representations of cytokine behaviors and properties.
source: However, previous models employed simplistic, non-spatial representations of cytokine behaviors and properties, which limited their ability to recapitulate cytokine alterations such as injection of transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) (Virgilio et al., 2021).
evidence: The authors cite a published study to support this claim about limitations of prior models.

claim: Prior muscle regeneration models did not include microvessel adaptations and dynamic extracellular matrix properties.
source: Furthermore, these prior models did not include microvessel adaptations and dynamic extracellular matrix (ECM) properties which are crucial for understanding the altered microenvironmental state following muscle injury.
evidence: The authors describe limitations of prior models based on their review of the literature.

claim: The model was implemented in CompuCell3D version 4.3.1.
source: We implemented the ABM in CompuCell3D (version 4.3.1), a Python-based modeling software (Swat et al., 2012).
evidence: The authors explicitly state the software platform used.

claim: The ABM spatially represents a 2D male murine skeletal muscle fascicle cross-section of approximately 50 muscle fibers.
source: The ABM spatially represents a 2D male murine skeletal muscle fascicle cross-section of approximately 50 muscle fibers (Figure 1).
evidence: The authors describe the model geometry and reference Figure 1.

claim: The ABM simulates the emergent phenomenon of muscle tissue from an acute injury over the course of 28 days.
source: The ABM simulates the emergent phenomenon of muscle tissue from an acute injury over the course of 28 days.
evidence: The authors describe the simulation timeframe.

claim: The ABM includes seven diffusing factors: HGF, MCP-1, MMP-9, TGF-β, TNF-α, VEGF-A, and IL-10.
source: In addition, the ABM includes seven diffusing factors, such as HGF, MCP-1, MMP-9, TGF-β, TNF-α, VEGF-A, and IL-10.
evidence: The authors list the cytokines included in the model.

claim: Each Monte Carlo step represents a 15 min timestep.
source: Each Monte Carlo step (mcs) represents a 15 min timestep, and the model simulations were run until 28 days post injury.
evidence: The authors specify the temporal resolution of the model.

claim: The model was run with 45 Cellular-Potts evaluations per mcs to ensure stability in migratory agent behavior.
source: The cell velocity is limited by how many times the Cellular-Potts algorithm is run, so we set 45 Cellular-Potts evaluations per mcs to ensure stability in migratory agent behavior.
evidence: The authors describe a technical parameter choice for model stability.

claim: Neutrophils are recruited through capillaries to sites of necrotic tissue.
source: Neutrophils are recruited through capillaries to sites of necrotic tissue (Table 1).
evidence: The authors describe neutrophil behavior in the model, referencing Table 1.

claim: Neutrophils move to areas of necrotic tissue with high concentrations of HGF by chemotaxing along the HGF gradient.
source: Neutrophils move to areas of necrotic tissue with high concentrations of HGF by chemotaxing along the HGF gradient to reach areas of necrosis (Madaro and Bouché, 2014; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The authors describe neutrophil chemotaxis behavior and cite supporting studies.

claim: Neutrophils phagocytose necrotic tissue and facilitate remodeling into ECM with low collagen density.
source: Neutrophils phagocytose necrotic tissue and facilitate remodeling into ECM with low collagen density.
evidence: The authors describe neutrophil function in the model.

claim: During phagocytosis, neutrophils secrete MMP-9, MCP-1, and TNF-α.
source: During phagocytosis, neutrophils secrete MMP-9, MCP-1, and TNF-α (Butterfield et al., 2006; Madaro and Bouché, 2014; Wang, 2018; Soehnlein et al., 2008).
evidence: The authors describe neutrophil secretion behavior and cite supporting studies.

claim: Individual neutrophil agents apoptose after phagocytosing two necrotic cells or 12.5 hr after their recruitment.
source: Individual neutrophil agents apoptose after phagocytosing two necrotic cells (based on calibration) or 12.5 hr after their recruitment (Fox et al., 2010).
evidence: The authors describe neutrophil apoptosis rules, citing a study for the time parameter.

claim: Resident macrophages are distributed randomly throughout the tissue at a ratio of 1 macrophage per 5 myofibers at model initialization.
source: Resident macrophages are distributed randomly throughout the tissue at a ratio of 1 macrophage per 5 myofibers at model initialization and secrete MCP-1 (Oishi and Manabe, 2018; Table 2).
evidence: The authors describe the initial macrophage distribution and cite a supporting study.

claim: Monocytes are recruited through healthy capillary microvasculature and chemotax along MCP-1, VEGF-A, TGF-β.
source: After tissue injury, monocytes are recruited through healthy capillary microvasculature and chemotax along MCP-1, VEGF-A, TGF-β (Kratofil et al., 2017; Chazaud et al., 2003; Owen and Mohamadzadeh, 2013; Reibman et al., 1991).
evidence: The authors describe monocyte recruitment and chemotaxis, citing supporting studies.

claim: Monocytes transition to M1 polarized macrophages when the monocyte agent experiences a large enough TNF-α concentration or if enough time has passed that a predefined transition time threshold is met.
source: Monocytes transition to M1 polarized macrophages when the monocyte agent experiences a large enough TNF-α concentration or if enough time has passed that a predefined transition time threshold is met. Each monocyte agent at creation has a defined transition time sampled from a Gaussian distribution with mean and SD set to reproduce literature-defined populations of M1 macrophages over time (Arnold et al., 2007; Mosser and Edwards, 2008).
evidence: The authors describe the monocyte to M1 transition rules and cite supporting studies.

claim: M1 macrophages may transition to M2 macrophages if the M1 macrophage agent experiences an IL-10 concentration that exceeds a threshold value or if the M1 macrophage has phagocytosed enough to meet a calibrated threshold value.
source: M1 macrophages may transition to M2 macrophages if the M1 macrophage agent experiences an IL-10 concentration that exceeds a threshold value or if the M1 macrophage has phagocytosed enough to meet a calibrated threshold value (as discussed in Model calibration) (Arnold et al., 2007; Saini et al., 2016; Das et al., 2015).
evidence: The authors describe the M1 to M2 transition rules and cite supporting studies.

claim: Following the transition to the anti-inflammatory phenotype, the M2 macrophages can proliferate, secrete TGF-β and IL-10, and chemotax along an MCP-1 gradient.
source: Following the transition to the anti-inflammatory phenotype, the M2 macrophages can proliferate, secrete TGF-β and IL-10, and chemotax along an MCP-1 gradient (Vogel et al., 2014; Arnold et al., 2007; Arabpour et al., 2021).
evidence: The authors describe M2 macrophage behaviors and cite supporting studies.

claim: The model is initialized with 1 quiescent SSC per every 4 fibers.
source: The model is initialized with 1 quiescent SSC per every 4 fibers and upon injury (Reimann et al., 2000).
evidence: The authors describe the initial SSC distribution and cite a supporting study.

claim: Additional SSCs are recruited based on the amount of HGF, MMP-9, and TGF-β.
source: Additional SSCs are recruited based on the amount of HGF, MMP-9, and TGF-β (Kawamura et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2009; Allen and Boxhorn, 1989; González et al., 2017; Table 3).
evidence: The authors describe SSC recruitment rules and cite supporting studies.

claim: For SSC activation there has to be enough HGF at the location of the quiescent SSC to induce activation.
source: For SSC activation there has to be enough HGF at the location of the quiescent SSC to induce activation (González et al., 2017; Allen et al., 1995; Miller et al., 2000; Tatsumi et al., 1998).
evidence: The authors describe SSC activation rules and cite supporting studies.

claim: Activated SSCs differentiated into myoblasts and myoblasts differentiate into myocytes.
source: Activated SSCs differentiated into myoblasts and myoblasts differentiate into myocytes (Cooper et al., 1999; Flamini et al., 2018; Bentzinger et al., 2012).
evidence: The authors describe SSC differentiation pathway and cite supporting studies.

claim: Myocytes can fuse to other myocytes to form new myotubes or fuse to fibers as long as the fiber is not fusion incompetent.
source: Myocytes can fuse to other myocytes to form new myotubes or fuse to fibers as long as the fiber is not fusion incompetent (i.e. fully necrotic) (Yin et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2019; Ruiz-Gómez et al., 2002).
evidence: The authors describe myocyte fusion rules and cite supporting studies.

claim: For model initialization, fibroblasts are randomly placed within the ECM at a population size that is proportional to the number of fibers.
source: For model initialization, fibroblasts are randomly placed within the ECM at a population size that is proportional to the number of fibers (Murphy et al., 2011; Table 4).
evidence: The authors describe the initial fibroblast distribution and cite a supporting study.

claim: Fibroblasts are activated based on the concentration of TGF-β around the fibroblast.
source: Fibroblasts are activated based on the concentration of TGF-β around the fibroblast (Beanes et al., 2003; Chellini et al., 2019).
evidence: The authors describe fibroblast activation rules and cite supporting studies.

claim: Fibroblasts can differentiate into myofibroblasts with extended exposure to TGF-β.
source: Fibroblasts divide when they are near dividing SSCs and can differentiate into myofibroblasts with extended exposure to TGF-β (Murphy et al., 2011; Desmoulière et al., 1993; Wipff et al., 2007).
evidence: The authors describe fibroblast differentiation rules and cite supporting studies.

claim: The muscle fascicle environment includes approximately 4 capillaries per fiber and 1 lymphatic vessel.
source: The muscle fascicle environment includes approximately 4 capillaries per fiber and 1 lymphatic vessel (Wickler, 1981; Gehlert et al., 2010; Table 6).
evidence: The authors describe the microvascular density and cite supporting studies.

claim: Capillaries that are neighboring areas of necrosis become non-perfused and therefore are unable to transport cells into the microenvironment until regenerated.
source: Capillaries that are neighboring areas of necrosis become non-perfused and therefore are unable to transport cells into the microenvironment until regenerated (Jacobsen et al., 2021).
evidence: The authors describe capillary damage rules and cite a supporting study.

claim: Angiogenesis can occur as long as there is enough VEGF-A present at the non-perfused capillary.
source: Angiogenesis can occur as long as there is enough VEGF-A present at the non-perfused capillary (Frey et al., 2012).
evidence: The authors describe angiogenesis rules and cite a supporting study.

claim: There is an increase in the capillary-to-myofiber ratio during muscle regeneration, which is due to the formation of new capillary sprouts modulated in part by local MMP-9 and VEGF-A levels.
source: Similar to published studies, there is an increase in the capillary-to-myofiber ratio during muscle regeneration, which is due to the formation of new capillary sprouts modulated in part by local MMP-9 and VEGF-A levels (Jacobsen et al., 2021; Hardy et al., 2016; Haas et al., 2000).
evidence: The authors describe capillary sprouting behavior and cite supporting studies.

claim: Initial ranges for the 52 unknown parameters were determined by literature review or by running the model to test possible upper and lower thresholds for parameters.
source: Initial ranges for the 52 unknown parameters were determined by literature review or by running the model to test possible upper and lower thresholds for parameters (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The authors describe the parameter initialization process.

claim: CaliPro was selected as the calibration method because it is model-agnostic, selects viable parameter ranges in the setting of a very high-dimensional parameter space, and circumvents the need for a cost function.
source: CaliPro was selected as the calibration method because it is model-agnostic which allows it to handle the complexities of stochastic models such as ABMs, selects viable parameter ranges in the setting of a very high-dimensional parameter space, and circumvents the need for a cost function, a challenge when there are many objectives, as in our case.
evidence: The authors justify their choice of calibration method.

claim: Latin hypercube sampling was used to generate 600 samples which were run in triplicate.
source: Briefly, Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) was used to generate 600 samples which were run in triplicate.
evidence: The authors describe the sampling strategy for calibration.

claim: Following eight iterations of narrowing the parameter space with CaliPro, a set of parameters was reached that had fewer passing runs than the previous iteration.
source: Following eight iterations of narrowing the parameter space with CaliPro, we reached a set of parameters that had fewer passing runs than the previous iteration.
evidence: The authors describe the iterative calibration process.

claim: The final parameter set was run 100 times to verify that the variation from the stochastic nature of the rules did not cause output that was inconsistent with experimental trends.
source: The final parameter set was run 100 times to verify that the variation from the stochastic nature of the rules did not cause output that was inconsistent with experimental trends.
evidence: The authors describe the validation of the final parameter set.

claim: Model outputs for M1, M2, and total macrophage counts, neutrophil counts, and capillary counts were compared with published experimental data to verify that these outputs followed trends from the experimental data without requiring extra model tuning.
source: We compared model outputs M1, M2, and total macrophage counts (Hardy et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018), neutrophil counts (Nguyen et al., 2011), and capillary counts (Ochoa et al., 2007) that were kept separate from the calibration criteria with published experimental data to verify that these outputs followed trends from the experimental data without requiring extra model tuning.
evidence: The authors describe the validation approach using independent datasets.

claim: One hundred replicates of each model perturbation were performed, and perturbation outputs were compared with control simulation outputs via a two-sample t-test with a significance level of 0.05.
source: One hundred replicates of each model perturbation were performed, and perturbation outputs were compared with control simulation outputs via a two-sample t-test with a significance level of 0.05.
evidence: The authors describe the statistical analysis approach for perturbations.

claim: The simulations captured SSC and fibroblast cellular behaviors, as well as CSA outcomes, that aligned with experimental studies.
source: Following parameter density-based calibration, the unknown parameters were narrowed into a final calibration parameter set (Supplementary file 1). The simulations captured SSC and fibroblast cellular behaviors, as well as CSA outcomes, that aligned with experimental studies (Figure 1; Figure 2; Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The authors report that calibration was successful, referencing figures showing alignment with data.

claim: The model data were consistent with the experimental trends, and the 95% confidence interval was within the standard deviation for all calibration data timepoints except for SSCs at day 3.
source: The model data were consistent with the experimental trends, and the 95% confidence interval was within the standard deviation (SD) for all calibration data timepoints except for SSCs at day 3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The authors report quantitative agreement between model and experimental data.

claim: The model reproduced findings from multiple studies, replicating how altered conditions lead to both improved and diminished muscle regeneration.
source: Overall, the model reproduced findings from multiple studies, replicating how altered conditions lead to both improved and diminished muscle regeneration (Figure 4).
evidence: The authors report that perturbation studies validated the model's predictive capabilities.

claim: Injections of VEGF-A led to faster CSA recovery, more damaged tissue clearance, and a concentration-dependent dose response, consistent with prior studies.
source: Injections of vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) led to faster CSA recovery, more damaged tissue clearance, and a concentration-dependent dose response, consistent with prior studies (Arsic et al., 2004).
evidence: The authors report model predictions that align with published experimental results.

claim: Cell depletion simulations predicted decrease in all markers of regeneration, consistent with prior studies.
source: Cell depletion simulations predicted decrease in all markers of regeneration, consistent with prior studies (Arsic et al., 2004; Teixeira et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The authors report model predictions that align with published experimental results.

claim: When simulating hindered angiogenesis conditions, the model aligned with experimental studies showing detriments in CSA recovery, increased neutrophil and macrophage cells, and elevated ECM collagen density.
source: When simulating hindered angiogenesis conditions, the model aligned with experimental studies showing detriments in CSA recovery, increased neutrophil and macrophage cells, and elevated ECM collagen density, indicating progression of fibrosis within the microenvironment (Hardy et al., 2019).
evidence: The authors report model predictions that align with published experimental results.

claim: Simulations of TNF-α knockout predicted increased CSA recovery, while experiments measured decreased recovery of CSA.
source: First, simulations of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) knockout (KO) predicted increased CSA recovery, while experiments measured decreased recovery of CSA.
evidence: The authors report a discrepancy between model predictions and experimental results.

claim: The difference between TNF-α KO model predictions and experimental results is likely due to the fact that the model did not include cross-regulation with interferons which are upregulated with TNF-α KO.
source: This difference is likely due to the fact that the model did not include cross-regulation with interferons which are upregulated with TNF-α KO (Cantaert et al., 2010).
evidence: The authors provide a hypothesis for the discrepancy, citing a relevant study.

claim: Macrophage depletion simulations predicted decreased TGF-β concentrations throughout the simulation while experiments measured an initial decrease in concentration followed by increased concentrations at days 7 and 14.
source: Second, macrophage depletion simulations predicted decreased TGF-β concentrations throughout the simulation while experiments measured an initial decrease in concentration followed by increased concentrations at days 7 and 14.
evidence: The authors report a discrepancy between model predictions and experimental results.

claim: The difference in macrophage depletion results may be due to the fact that macrophage depletion was experimentally induced with clodronate-containing liposomes which could have reduced consistency of depletion across the time course and other downstream impacts that were not represented by decreasing macrophages in the model perturbation.
source: This difference may be due to the fact that macrophage depletion was experimentally induced with clodronate-containing liposomes which could have reduced consistency of depletion across the time course and other downstream impacts that were not represented by decreasing macrophages in the model perturbation (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The authors provide a hypothesis for the discrepancy, citing a relevant study.

claim: VEGF-A levels remained elevated compared to control simulations following the injection at day 5 post injury.
source: VEGF-A levels remained elevated compared to control simulations following the injection at day 5 post injury (Figure 5A).
evidence: The authors report model predictions from VEGF-A injection simulations.

claim: CSA recovery had the highest increase at 28 days post injury with the high VEGF-A injection followed by the extra high injection.
source: CSA recovery had the highest increase at 28 days post injury with the high (103 relative concentration delivered) VEGF-A injection followed by the extra high (2×103 relative concentration delivered) injection (Figure 5B).
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing a dose-response relationship.

claim: The medium and low VEGF-A injections had higher CSA recovery 15 days post injury but were not significantly different from the control at day 28.
source: The medium (750 relative concentration delivered) and low (500 relative concentration delivered) VEGF-A injections had higher CSA recovery 15 days post injury but were not significantly different from the control at day 28.
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing temporal differences in dose response.

claim: All VEGF-A injections had a higher capillary count and were proportional to the level of VEGF-A injection.
source: All VEGF-A injections had a higher capillary count and were proportional to the level of VEGF-A injection (Figure 5C).
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing a dose-response relationship for capillaries.

claim: The impact of VEGF-A injection on peak SSC and fibroblast counts was dependent on dosage amount, with the extra high VEGF-A injection resulting in the largest peaks.
source: The impact of VEGF-A injection on peak SSC and fibroblast counts was dependent on dosage amount, with the extra high VEGF-A injection resulting in the largest peaks (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing dose-dependent effects on cell counts.

claim: HGF levels were elevated from days 5 to 28 with hindered angiogenesis, as were TGF-β and IL-10.
source: In contrast, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) levels were elevated from days 5 to 28 with hindered angiogenesis, as were TGF-β and interleukin 10 (IL-10) (Figure 5I and L).
evidence: The authors report model predictions for cytokine dynamics under hindered angiogenesis.

claim: MCP-1 concentration had a lower overall peak level with elevated levels from days 21 to 28 under hindered angiogenesis.
source: Monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) concentration had a lower overall peak level with elevated levels from days 21 to 28 (Figure 5H).
evidence: The authors report model predictions for MCP-1 dynamics under hindered angiogenesis.

claim: Hindered angiogenesis had lower CSA recovery throughout the simulation and did not achieve unaltered regeneration levels.
source: Hindered angiogenesis had lower CSA recovery throughout the simulation and did not achieve unaltered regeneration levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing impaired recovery with hindered angiogenesis.

claim: With MCP-1 KO there was an overall increase in cytokine levels for all other cytokines within the microenvironment except for VEGF-A at 12 hr post injury.
source: For example, with MCP-1 KO there was an overall increase in cytokine levels for all other cytokines within the microenvironment except for VEGF-A at 12 hr post injury (Figure 6A).
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing cytokine cross-talk.

claim: With TNF-α KO there was a decrease in TGF-β at early timepoints but a strong increase by day 28.
source: With TNF-α KO there was a decrease in TGF-β at early timepoints but a strong increase by day 28 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing temporal cytokine dynamics.

claim: Following IL-10 KO there was an increase in TNF-α that peaked at 7 days post injury.
source: Following IL-10 KO there was an increase in TNF-α that peaked at 7 days post injury (Figure 6C).
evidence: The authors report model predictions showing cytokine cross-talk.

claim: Latin hypercube sampling-PRCC of cytokine decay and diffusion parameters elucidated temporal relationships between cytokine parameters and key regeneration metrics, such as positive correlations between CSA and TGF-β and MMP-9 decay.
source: Latin hypercube sampling (LHS)-PRCC of cytokine decay and diffusion parameters elucidated temporal relationships between cytokine parameters and key regeneration metrics, such as positive correlations between CSA and TGF-β and MMP-9 decay (Table 9).
evidence: The authors report sensitivity analysis results identifying key parameter relationships.

claim: Of all cytokine parameters, the model outputs were most sensitive to HGF decay, with all outputs except M1 cell count being significantly impacted.
source: Of all cytokine parameters, the model outputs were most sensitive to HGF decay, with all outputs except M1 cell count being significantly impacted.
evidence: The authors report sensitivity analysis results identifying the most influential parameter.

claim: PRCC plots showed that TGF-β and MMP decay were positively correlated and HGF decay was negatively correlated with CSA recovery, with higher significance at timepoints after 12 days.
source: PRCC plots showed that TGF-β and MMP decay were positively correlated and HGF decay was negatively correlated with CSA recovery, with higher significance at timepoints after 12 days (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The authors report sensitivity analysis results showing temporal parameter correlations.

claim: All tested cytokine alterations except higher MCP-1 decay resulted in higher CSA recovery compared to the control.
source: All tested alterations except higher monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) decay resulted in higher cross-sectional area (CSA) recovery compared to the control (A).
evidence: The authors report results from in silico perturbation experiments, referencing Figure 7A.

claim: The combined cytokine alteration resulted in the highest CSA recovery.
source: The combined cytokine alteration resulted in the highest CSA recovery (Figure 7A), as well as increased M1 macrophage counts (Figure 7B), decreased M2 macrophage counts (Figure 7C), increased fibroblasts (Figure 7D) and SSCs cell counts (Figure 7E).
evidence: The authors report results showing synergistic effects of combined cytokine perturbations.

claim: Capillaries regenerated faster in the combined perturbation than under unaltered conditions.
source: Capillaries regenerated faster in the combined perturbation than under unaltered conditions (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The authors report results showing improved angiogenesis with combined perturbations.

claim: The combined cytokine perturbation predicted a 13% improvement in CSA recovery compared to the unaltered regeneration amount at 28 days.
source: The combined cytokine perturbation predicted a 13% improvement in CSA recovery compared to the unaltered regeneration amount at 28 days.
evidence: The authors report a quantitative prediction from the combined perturbation simulation.

claim: The combined cytokine perturbation had higher peaks in SSC and fibroblast counts than any of the singular cytokine perturbations, indicating the synergistic effects of altering the cytokine dynamics in combination.
source: The combined cytokine perturbation also had higher peaks in SSC and fibroblast counts than any of the singular cytokine perturbations, indicating the synergistic effects of altering the cytokine dynamics in combination.
evidence: The authors interpret the results as evidence of synergistic effects.

claim: The model provides a more controlled environment for studying muscle regeneration, reducing error and variation commonly encountered with in vivo experiments.
source: The creation of the model provides a more controlled environment for studying muscle regeneration, reducing error and variation commonly encountered with in vivo experiments.
evidence: The authors discuss an advantage of the computational modeling approach.

claim: The ability for altered cytokine concentrations to change regeneration outcomes is consistent with studies that have found enhanced muscle recovery with delivery of platelet-rich plasma which contain VEGF and TGF-β.
source: The ability for altered cytokine concentrations to change regeneration outcomes is consistent with studies that have found enhanced muscle recovery with delivery of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) which contain VEGF and TGF- β (Kunze et al., 2019).
evidence: The authors relate their findings to published experimental studies.

claim: Perturbations varying VEGF-A injection doses showed increased CSA recovery up to a threshold (high VEGF-A injection simulation), beyond which further improvements in CSA recovery cease.
source: Perturbations varying VEGF-A injection doses showed increased CSA recovery up to a threshold (high VEGF-A injection simulation), beyond which further improvements in CSA recovery cease.
evidence: The authors report a nonlinear dose-response relationship from model simulations.

claim: Cytokine KO simulations revealed the complex nature of the relationship between cytokines; removal of one cytokine from the system has a cascading temporal impact.
